mcqs.question: You need to check membership repeatedly against the same collection inside a loop. What's the standard fix if that collection starts as a plain list?
options: Sort the list once, since sorted lists support O(1) membership checks
Convert it to a hash set once up front, so each membership check becomes O(1) expected instead of an O(n) scan
Reverse the list so recently checked elements are found faster
Nothing changes — list membership checks are already O(1)
mcqs.explanation: Building the set once costs O(n), but every subsequent membership check drops from an O(n) scan to expected O(1) — the classic space-for-time trade. Sorting doesn't make membership O(1) on its own; it only enables binary search at O(log n).

mcqs.question: Why does computing the intersection of two hash sets run in O(min(n, m)) rather than O(n·m)?
options: Because sets automatically remove duplicates before comparing
Because you walk the smaller set once and test each element for O(1) membership in the larger set, instead of comparing every pair across both collections
Because hash sets store their elements in sorted order
Because intersection only works when both sets are the same size
mcqs.explanation: Walking the smaller set and doing an O(1) membership check per element against the larger set avoids the pairwise comparison a nested loop over two lists would require. Hash sets have no guaranteed sort order, and set size doesn't need to match.

mcqs.question: Why does the "seen so far" hash-set pattern beat sorting-then-scanning-for-adjacent-duplicates for detecting any duplicate in an array?
options: It uses less memory in every case
Sorting cannot detect duplicates at all
It runs in O(n) versus sorting's O(n log n), since each set check-and-insert is O(1) expected while sorting pays a log-factor
It preserves the sorted order of the input, which sorting destroys
mcqs.explanation: A single pass with O(1) expected set operations is strictly O(n), beating any comparison-based sort's O(n log n) floor. Sorting can detect duplicates fine via adjacency — it's just asymptotically slower here — and the set approach uses more memory, not less.

mcqs.question: In the Longest Consecutive Sequence algorithm, why do you only start counting a run from numbers where `x - 1` is not in the set?
options: It's an arbitrary optimization that happens to also be correct
Because numbers with a predecessor present are guaranteed to be duplicates
So that only true sequence starts begin an inner loop, keeping each number visited a bounded number of times and the whole algorithm linear
Because the set only stores numbers with no predecessor
mcqs.explanation: Skipping non-starts means the inner while-loop only ever runs from the beginning of each run, so across the whole pass every number is touched a constant number of times — that's what keeps the nested-looking loop at O(n) instead of O(n^2). It isn't about duplicates or set contents.

mcqs.question: You need to dedup a huge array but memory is the binding constraint, not speed. Which approach fits better, and why?
options: A hash set, because it always uses less memory than sorting
Sorting in place, since it needs only O(1) extra space versus a hash set's O(n)
A hash set, because sorting cannot handle duplicate values
Neither — both approaches require identical memory
mcqs.explanation: An in-place sort followed by an adjacent-duplicate scan needs no extra collection at all, while a hash set inherently costs O(n) extra memory to hold the seen values. Sorting handles duplicates naturally via adjacency after sorting.
